title: Boreendo: a small instrument and a large safeguarding task
summary: Safeguarding the boreendo means sustaining makers, players and opportunities to learn—not merely preserving a small clay instrument in a display.

body.text: The boreendo is small enough for its visual simplicity to conceal the work around it. A hollow clay body with sound holes may appear to be a modest object. Yet making it sound, shaping its musical possibilities and teaching someone else to use it involve knowledge that cannot be preserved by keeping the object alone.

UNESCO’s boreendo record describes clay that is dried and fired, with sound produced by blowing and altered through the handling of the openings and mouthpiece. It also notes recent modifications that extend musical possibilities. This is evidence of an instrument being worked with and developed, not a form that must remain physically unchanged to count as heritage.

The element was inscribed in 2025 on the List of Intangible Cultural Heritage in Need of Urgent Safeguarding. The decision records community participation in the nomination and calls for continued involvement in safeguarding, with particular attention to education. Recognition is therefore connected to a task, not a declaration that the task has been completed.
Follow the work beyond the finished object

A display can identify the material and shape of a boreendo. To understand the craft, a record also needs the maker’s explanation of decisions: how the body is formed, how openings are handled and how a finished piece is judged. Such documentation should distinguish what a particular maker demonstrates from a universal rule for every instrument.

Playing introduces another kind of expertise. An object that produces a sound does not automatically reveal the repertoire or the control needed for performance. A short demonstration may attract attention while leaving the process of learning almost entirely invisible. Repeated lessons, feedback and opportunities to play can matter more than a single public appearance.

UNESCO’s account describes transmission within families and newer teaching settings, including schools and cultural events. These settings raise practical questions. Who has time to teach? Can learners obtain suitable instruments? Is there a place to practise? Which forms of support do the people involved consider useful? A safeguarding plan becomes meaningful through such details.
Avoid the romance of disappearance

Calling an instrument the last trace of an ancient civilization may produce a dramatic caption, but it requires evidence that a contemporary performance cannot supply. Likewise, a dated statement about the number of expert practitioners should not be repeated indefinitely as a current census. Attention is more useful when it remains accurate.

The people who make, decorate, teach and perform should be credited for their particular contributions. Roles recorded in one nomination should not become permanent restrictions on who may participate. The point of safeguarding is to support a living practice, including the choices its participants make about its future.

The boreendo’s scale makes this lesson especially clear. A museum case can protect a clay object from damage. Sustaining the heritage around it requires relationships, learning and material support outside the case. The instrument deserves to be seen, but also understood as something people continue to make meaningful through use.

title: The rubab as an instrument made and maintained
summary: The rubab’s sound depends on craft, setup and continuing care. A museum object and a regional safeguarding record reveal different parts of that work.

body.text: A rubab is not only a recognizable outline or a sound associated with a region. It is also a made object whose parts must work together. Looking at its materials and the knowledge required to maintain it changes the emphasis from a picturesque performance to the labour that makes performance possible.

The Metropolitan Museum of Art holds a rubab catalogued as Pakistani, with Karachi given as its geographical association and a date in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Its recorded materials include wood, skin, gut, bone and mother-of-pearl. This is the description of one object, not a universal specification for every rubab made or played in Pakistan.

The combination is instructive. Decorative inlay and sounding components belong to the same instrument but do different work. A collection photograph, where available, may make ornament easy to notice while giving little information about the condition of the strings, the setup or how the instrument was played.
Craft is a relationship with sound

UNESCO’s 2024 inscription on crafting and playing rubab/rabab describes skills including woodwork, carving and inlay, transmitted through practical learning. The participating states are Afghanistan, Iran, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Pakistan is not listed in that nomination; the record is a regional comparison, not a UNESCO designation for Pakistani rubab practice.

For an individual instrument, a useful account would follow the maker’s decisions rather than replacing them with a generic list of materials. How is the intended use discussed with a player? What adjustments are made before the instrument is considered ready? Which parts are expected to be replaced through use? These questions connect craft with the experience of musicians.

Maintenance belongs in the story too. An instrument can remain visually impressive while no longer being suitable to play. Conversely, a working instrument may show replacement parts and ordinary wear. Neither appearance alone tells us whether it has been well cared for or what a conservator or maker would recommend.
Museum care and musical use are different decisions

A historic collection object should not be made playable merely to satisfy curiosity. Its materials, condition and significance require specialist assessment. A musician’s working rubab has different needs, and decisions about repair should involve someone with appropriate expertise. An introductory heritage article cannot replace that judgement.

An archive can still make maintenance visible by recording repairs, modifications and the names of craftspeople when those facts are known. It should distinguish a maker’s original work from later intervention. If an instrument has travelled between musicians or regions, that history can be as revealing as an assigned geographical label.

The most complete account therefore connects an object record with testimony from makers and players, while respecting the limits of each source. Hearing the rubab then means hearing more than a regional emblem. It means recognizing the accumulated decisions, skilled hands and continuing care through which a piece of crafted material becomes a musical companion.

title: The alghoza and the coordination of breath
summary: The alghoza’s paired pipes ask a player to coordinate airflow and melody. Its sound is best understood through specific musicians rather than a single regional stereotype.

body.text: Two pipes held together can create an impression of effortless continuity. The alghoza’s effect is more interesting when we notice the coordination behind it: air, finger movement and the relationship between sustained and changing sound. The instrument is not simply a pair of flutes added together; it is a way of making their interaction musically useful.

The American Institute of Pakistan Studies describes paired flutes under several names, including alghoza, pava and beenu in Sindh, and a related doneli form in Balochistan. It notes that the pipes can differ in length. These descriptions establish a family of practices, not proof that every named form is identical in construction, tuning or use.

A comparative example comes from Jodhpur RIFF’s programme for Taga Ram Bhil in Rajasthan. Its account emphasizes circular breathing, with one pipe sustaining a note while the other carries melodic phrases, and identifies the musician as an instrument maker as well as a performer. This is a documented account of a particular artist’s practice across the border, not a template imposed on all Pakistani players.
Continuity is something to listen for

The phrase circular breathing refers to a technique for sustaining airflow while replenishing breath. A listener does not need to master it to appreciate what it makes possible. Begin by noticing whether the sound continues across a long phrase and how movement in the melody relates to the steadier tone beside it.

Then attend to changes rather than continuity alone. Where does a phrase gather energy? When does a repeated figure return? Does the balance between the two pipes remain constant? These questions direct attention to musical choices rather than treating sustained sound as a physical trick performed for an audience.

A recording can help repeated listening, but its conditions matter. A close microphone may emphasize breath or small attacks differently from an outdoor performance. Editing can alter the impression of duration. Unless the record documents a continuous take, a listener should not use its length as a measure of how long a musician played without interruption.
Credit the person behind the sound

Names, repertoire and learning histories make a stronger introduction than a broad caption such as desert music. A performer may identify teachers, describe how an instrument was made or explain why a particular tune suits an occasion. Those details need to be recorded with permission rather than inferred from clothing or scenery.

Comparing instruments also requires restraint. A similar appearance does not establish a shared tuning, and a shared name does not settle the question of origin. Where sources disagree, an archive can preserve the competing descriptions without inventing a single migration story to make the map look tidy.

The alghoza rewards a kind of listening that follows several things at once. The paired sound is immediately attractive; its deeper interest lies in the control that keeps those parts in conversation. Recognizing that work gives the musician room to be an artist and craftsperson, not merely the bearer of an atmospheric regional sound.

title: Surando and the relationship between instrument and voice
summary: A surando record should explain both the instrument and its musical role. Bowed strings, regional names and relationships with singing need precise attribution.

body.text: A bowed instrument can seem to follow a voice closely enough that a listener describes it as singing. That resemblance is a useful starting point, but it should not replace attention to what an instrument actually does. In a surando performance, the relationship between sustained tone, melodic movement and any accompanying voice needs to be heard in a specific musical setting.

The Hartenberger collection records a surando associated with Kutch, describing a wooden body, a skin-covered part of the soundbox and several kinds of strings. Its account distinguishes bowed, drone and sympathetic strings on the catalogued object. This is a comparative instrument record from India; it does not establish the construction of every surando used in Sindh.

The American Institute of Pakistan Studies connects the name surando with Sindh and related names, including saro and saroz, with other regions of Pakistan. Such naming is a reason to ask more precise questions, not to collapse every similarly named instrument into one unchanging design.
What does accompaniment mean?

In his historical account of Balochistan’s music, Mohammad-Taqi Masudiya describes sung narrative with a bowed sorud and a plucked lute providing a rhythmic drone. The account identifies distinct musical roles. It should not be generalized into a claim that a surando always accompanies singing in exactly that combination.

For a listener, accompaniment can be investigated at the scale of a phrase. Does the instrument move with the singer, answer after a line or sustain a sound while the voice pauses? Does a repeated figure connect sections? A performance may make more than one of these relationships audible. Describing the actual exchange is more informative than saying only that the instrument imitates the human voice.

If there is no singer, the question changes rather than disappears. An instrumental performance may draw on a familiar vocal melody, but that connection needs identification by a performer or reliable record. A listener’s impression of speech-like phrasing is not by itself evidence of a particular song.
Keep construction and performance connected

A museum catalogue can describe strings and materials while leaving the intended tuning uncertain. A recording can reveal musical behaviour while showing little of the instrument’s construction. Combining the two types of evidence requires an identified connection, not merely a similar-looking photograph chosen to illustrate the sound.

The same applies to regional labels. A musician’s location, the place an instrument was made and the origin attributed to a repertoire may differ. Recording those fields separately helps preserve a history of exchange. It also prevents an instrument from being assigned to a single modern boundary simply because that makes an archive easier to browse.

A strong introduction to the surando therefore makes room for both the object and the encounter. It credits maker and player where known, explains the source of its names and follows the instrument’s role in a documented performance. The apparent closeness to the voice then becomes a question worth listening to, rather than an attractive description repeated without evidence.

title: Dambura traditions and the risk of a single regional label
summary: Dambura and related names occur across different musical settings. Comparing Baloch and Afghan records shows why a single regional label can mislead.

body.text: An instrument name can travel farther than a single design or playing tradition. Dambura is a good example of why a heritage archive should resist assigning one label to one province and treating the matter as settled. Similar names may connect instruments while still leaving important differences in construction, repertoire and musical role.

In his account of Balochistan’s music, Mohammad-Taqi Masudiya describes a long-necked plucked dambura providing a rhythmic drone alongside bowed accompaniment in sung narrative. The emphasis is on what the instrument contributes to that performance. The article, first published in 1988, should be read as a historically situated account rather than a current inventory of every Baloch musician.

Smithsonian Folkways’ notes for recordings from Afghanistan describe a dambura as a two-stringed, fretless plucked lute associated particularly with the north of that country. This provides a useful comparison, but it would be a mistake to transfer that exact description automatically to every instrument bearing a related name in Balochistan.
Compare the object before merging the labels

Begin with visible and documented features. What is the shape of the body? How many strings are present on this instrument? Are there frets? What does its maker or player call it? If those answers are missing, a broad name is not enough to fill them in confidently.

Next ask about musical function. An instrument that supplies a recurring rhythmic support in one setting may carry a melody or accompany a solo singer in another. Similar construction does not require identical use. Conversely, instruments with different forms can occupy comparable roles within different ensembles.

The recording notes matter because they connect description with identifiable tracks and musicians. An isolated image labelled folk lute can show an object without telling us what was played on it. A sound file labelled Balochistan may tell us even less about the instrument if it lacks performer and recording information.
A region contains more than one community

Balochistan is not a synonym for a single language or musical practice. An archive should distinguish a geographical association from the language of a song and from the identity a performer gives to their work. Those distinctions are especially important when a familiar instrument name encourages a quick, overly broad classification.

Claims about ancestry also need evidence. A resemblance between names or shapes is not a complete history of transmission. It may suggest a question for research, but it does not establish when an instrument arrived, who carried it or whether one community borrowed directly from another.

The practical goal is not to abandon regional browsing. It is to make the label an entry point into a more exact record. A dambura article becomes stronger when it identifies the particular instrument and source, explains its musical role and leaves unsupported connections open. Listeners can then explore relationships across the region without losing the distinct practices that give those relationships substance.

title: The dhol in work, celebration and performance
summary: The dhol’s force comes from musical choices and social occasions as well as volume. A player’s account shows tradition as something learned and continually reworked.

body.text: A dhol can announce its presence before the player comes into view. Yet describing it only as loud misses the musical decisions that make its sound meaningful: placement of strokes, changes in emphasis and the relationship between a drummer and the people moving or listening nearby. The drum belongs to an occasion, not just to a volume level.

In an essay for the Smithsonian, musician Sunny Jain describes the dhol as a double-headed wooden drum associated with farming, dance and special events in Punjabi life. He also discusses his interest in Pakistani Sufi dhol players after joining Junoon. This is a musician’s account of learning and influence, with named artists rather than an anonymous picture of regional tradition.

Jain’s own practice brings those influences into conversation with jazz and other music. He describes using electronic effects as well as acoustic sound. His account is useful not because it defines every dhol tradition, but because it shows a player making deliberate choices about what to inherit and how to work with it.
Listen for relationship, not just repetition

A repeated pattern can establish a framework in which a small change becomes significant. Notice when a player intensifies a phrase, leaves space or signals a return. The response of dancers or fellow musicians can help explain the effect, but it should not be assumed from an isolated audio clip.

Different settings also change what is audible. A drum in a procession competes with movement and surrounding sound. A microphone on a stage can present a different balance. A studio recording may isolate details that a nearby listener at an outdoor gathering would hear as part of a larger event.

An archival Smithsonian record from the 1976 Festival of American Folklife identifies a Pakistani programme that includes a Punjab folk tune with shehnai and dhol. That kind of entry offers a useful anchor: an occasion, a performance grouping and a record that can be investigated. It does not describe every use of the drum in Punjab.
Keep the work of the drummer visible

A cultural caption should credit the player and identify the setting whenever those facts are known. If a piece is associated with work, celebration or devotion, explain the basis of that association. Avoid turning a broad historical connection into an unsupported claim that the specific recording accompanied agricultural labour or a ritual.

The same care applies to change. A contemporary arrangement is not automatically a loss of tradition, just as an old-looking performance is not automatically faithful to a single original form. The musician’s account of learning, repertoire and intention can reveal a more complex relationship.

The dhol’s cultural power is not diminished by such precision. Its sound can bring people together while remaining the result of individual skill and shared expectations. Listening to those decisions allows a heritage archive to present a working musical practice—energetic, adaptable and situated—rather than a generic beat attached to every image of Punjabi celebration.

title: Polo in Baltistan: rules, memory and public space
summary: Polo grounds in Baltistan are spaces of activity and public memory. Historic places and current tournaments need to be connected without inventing one universal set of rules.

body.text: A polo ground may look like an open space when no match is underway. Its heritage value becomes clearer when that apparent emptiness is understood as room for activity: players crossing the field, spectators finding a place and a town gathering around an event. In Baltistan, the ground deserves attention alongside the dramatic images of horses and riders.

Virsapur’s linked record identifies Khaplu Polo Ground through the Department of Archaeology and Museums catalogue. It places a sporting space within the heritage inventory rather than limiting that inventory to enclosed buildings. The record does not, by itself, establish a complete history of matches or the rules used at every period.

Contemporary evidence offers another view. Gilgit-Baltistan’s tourism and culture department reports the conclusion of the 2026 Ali Sher Khan Anchan tournament at Maqpoon Polo Ground in Skardu. That is a different ground and a specific event. Keeping the two places distinct lets a reader connect historic sporting landscapes with continuing organized competition without inventing a direct event history for Khaplu.
Freestyle does not mean without expectations

Official tourism material describes freestyle polo as part of Gilgit-Baltistan’s sporting culture. Promotional phrases about minimal rules should not be read as proof that players recognize no conventions or responsibilities. A visitor needs the explanation of the particular organizers, not a generalized claim that the game is simply unregulated.

Ask how teams are constituted, how play begins and resumes, and how disputed moments are handled at the event being watched. These questions make a match easier to follow without importing the regulations of an unrelated polo competition. An archive should identify the date and source of any rules it records, because practice can vary.

The field itself is also evidence. Its entrances, edges and relationship to surrounding buildings can shape how people arrive and watch. Historical photographs may help trace changes, but an attractive image is not enough to establish a ground’s original dimensions or continuous use.
Preserve the capacity to gather

For a sporting landscape, conservation is not only about retaining an outline on a map. Questions about access, maintenance and competing uses affect whether the place can continue to support activity. A ground kept visually open but unavailable to players has a different relationship to living practice from one used regularly.

Spectators also have responsibilities. Follow the organizers’ boundaries and do not enter a playing area for a closer photograph. Familiarity among local participants should not be mistaken for permission to stand wherever a visitor chooses. Horses and fast-moving play require attention beyond the view through a phone.

Polo in Baltistan is therefore best approached through connected but distinct records: a place, a match, the people who organize it and the memories participants attach to it. Together they reveal a cultural landscape in use. None needs to be inflated into a claim that all mountain polo follows one timeless and identical tradition.

title: Tent pegging as a performed skill
summary: Tent pegging combines riding, timing and precision within organized competition. Understanding the skill means looking beyond the dramatic instant when a target is lifted.

body.text: The most photographed moment in tent pegging is brief: a rider reaches down, the weapon meets a small target and the target is carried away. That instant can make the event look like a feat of daring alone. A closer account sees coordination between horse and rider, preparation of the course and a competition structure that makes precision assessable.

The International Tent Pegging Federation describes the sport as a mounted discipline using a lance or sword to lift and carry a ground target. This provides a practical definition without requiring an uncertain origin story to explain every present-day event. A sporting action can have a historical association while its current organization follows a distinct set of rules.

The Equestrian Federation of Pakistan identifies the organization and promotion of tent pegging among its purposes. That institutional setting matters: local enthusiasm and international competition are connected through clubs, organizers and officials, not merely through the resemblance of one rider’s action to another’s.
Watch the run as a whole

For a spectator, the approach to the target is part of the performance. Notice the line of travel, the moment of reaching and what happens after contact. A successful-looking strike in a photograph does not show the full run or establish its official result. The score depends on the rules and judging of the competition being observed.

The ITPF rulebook effective in January 2019 illustrates the range of organization involved. It separates individual and team events, equipment, course arrangements, timekeeping, judging and veterinary matters. It is a dated document, not a claim about the exact regulations governing every event in 2026. Its value here is to show that the sport extends well beyond a single target.

A visitor who wants to follow a current competition should consult its published conditions or organizers. Weapon type, event format and scoring should not be guessed from clothing or a general festival description. Where commentary is available, it can help connect what is visible with the decisions officials make.
Horse care belongs inside the heritage account

The animal is not scenery around a human achievement. Preparation, handling and welfare are fundamental to the event. The presence of veterinary and horse-abuse provisions in formal rules makes that responsibility explicit. A cultural account should not celebrate a dramatic image while ignoring how the horse is treated.

Nor should an introductory article offer instructions for attempting the skill without appropriate training and supervision. For an ordinary visitor, the relevant guidance is to respect barriers, keep clear of the course and follow event staff. Photographs should be made from permitted positions, not by stepping into the line of a run.

Tent pegging becomes more impressive, not less, when its organization is visible. We can appreciate the precision of the rider while also recognizing the work of trainers, handlers, officials and course teams. The result is a portrait of a demanding contemporary sport with cultural associations, rather than a timeless spectacle reduced to a single spectacular second.

title: Traditional wrestling and the institution of the akhara
summary: An akhara is sustained by space, teaching and support as well as physical skill. Institutional evidence helps move its history beyond nostalgia about famous wrestlers.

body.text: A wrestling bout displays strength and technique, but the institution that prepares wrestlers is less visible in the moment of competition. The akhara is a place of practice, instruction and repeated work. Understanding it as an institution shifts attention from a few celebrated champions to the conditions that allow people to learn and continue.

A University of the Punjab press release records the opening of an akhara at its New Campus hostel grounds in May 2013. The ceremony included wrestlers and sports officials, followed by competitions. This is a specific example of institutional support: a place was provided and an activity organized. It does not establish that all traditional wrestling was flourishing or declining at the same rate.

A historical study by Tayyab Butt examines akharas in Lahore and Gujranwala through patronage and changing economic conditions. Its argument links difficulties in sustaining the institution with changes in support and everyday livelihoods. This is more useful as a question to investigate than a blanket statement that modernity inevitably destroys tradition.
Training needs a durable setting

A heritage record of an akhara should ask who teaches, who can attend and how the space is maintained. These practical details can reveal more about continuity than a claim that the practice is centuries old. A name may remain well known while the arrangements that once supported regular training have changed.

The relationship between teacher and learner also deserves careful documentation. How is a beginner introduced? What expectations accompany participation? Which aspects of the teaching are described as inherited, and which have been adapted? Answers should come from people involved rather than from assumptions imported from a different region’s wrestling literature.

A public competition and a training ground are not interchangeable records. The event may draw a large audience while the institution works quietly through ordinary days. Photographs of a successful bout cannot establish the frequency of practice, the availability of instruction or the costs borne by participants.
Look beyond a story of inevitable loss

Accounts of decline can draw attention to real pressures, but they can also make current practitioners disappear behind nostalgia. The university example shows why evidence needs dates and locations. An arena can open in one setting while another closes elsewhere. Both events may belong to the same wider history.

Likewise, supporting an akhara does not mean endorsing every practice attributed to it. Questions of access, safety and the treatment of learners remain relevant. A cultural description should not turn a wrestler’s diet or training routine into general health advice, and it should not assume that customs are identical across institutions.

The strongest account connects space, instruction, competition and support without collapsing them into one romantic image. It credits the people who sustain ordinary practice as well as those who win public recognition. Seen this way, the akhara is neither merely a patch of earth nor a relic awaiting rescue. It is an organization whose continuing life depends on concrete relationships and choices.

title: Children’s games as a changing archive
summary: Children’s games are transmitted by playing and negotiating, not just by preserving rules. Research in Chitral shows how documentation can support use while allowing adaptation.

body.text: A children’s game can survive without a printed rulebook because players teach it to one another. They demonstrate a movement, argue over a boundary, change a rule to fit the available space and invite someone new to join. That activity makes games a changing archive rather than a collection of instructions waiting to be copied exactly.

Rubina Nawab’s research at Aga Khan University offers a grounded example from Chitral. The project interviewed ten community elders, involved early-childhood education specialists in reviewing the material and selected seven games for classroom use. The choices considered age, inclusion and practicality rather than assuming that every remembered game would suit every group of children.

The study was carried out in a particular early-years class and used observation, reflection and discussion through successive cycles. Its findings concern that educational setting; they should not be inflated into a universal claim that any traditional game automatically produces the same developmental benefits. The value of the project includes the careful process of selection and adaptation.
A rule is only part of the record

To document a game, record what players call it, what materials they use and how play begins and ends. Then ask how they learned it and whether they know other versions. A disagreement about a rule may be valuable evidence of variation rather than a problem that the researcher must resolve into one official form.

Space matters too. A game played in a courtyard may be adjusted for a school ground or a narrow lane. The number and age of players can change what is practical. Describing those conditions helps a later reader understand the version recorded, instead of assuming that a short list of actions will reproduce the whole experience.

The 2025 publication Echoes of Play, by Nawab and Fozia Parveen, identifies traditional outdoor games of Chitral’s mountain communities as its subject. Its existence shows documentation being made into an educational resource. A book can support transmission, but it cannot replace the social work children do when they actually play.
Let children contribute to the archive

Adults’ memories are important, yet they should not be the only authority. Children may know variants, new names or solutions that make a game workable now. Recording those contributions avoids presenting change as evidence that they have failed to preserve the past correctly.

Ethical documentation is especially important here. Permission for research or a school activity is not automatically permission to publish identifiable photographs or recordings of children. A description of rules can often be shared without exposing names, faces or precise everyday locations. Participation should also allow a child to decline being recorded.

The aim is a resource that makes play possible, not a museum of compulsory authenticity. A well-documented game can carry a history while remaining open to thoughtful adaptation. Its heritage continues when children find it worth playing together—and when an archive respects their role as present-day makers of that experience, rather than treating them only as recipients of adult memory.
